summary: Learners plot and read positions in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane using positive and negative x- and y-values. The core idea: a position is an ordered pair whose FIRST coordinate is read along the horizontal x-axis and whose SECOND is read along the vertical y-axis, with each sign tied to a direction. Build the plane as two perpendicular number lines crossing at the origin so negatives inherit the ordering the child already knows, teach the axis-order convention structurally (not via a first-quadrant rhyme), and work across all four quadrants together rather than adding negatives afterwards.
misconceptions: Reverses the ordered pair, plotting/reading (y, x) — takes the vertical value first (the single most common coordinate error).
Sign/direction error: counts the wrong way for a negative value, landing a point in the wrong quadrant.
Misreads the scale: assumes each grid line is one unit when it is 2, 5 or 10, or reads two differently-scaled axes as if identical.
Over-relies on the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic and is stranded when a coordinate is negative (goes 'up the stairs' for a negative y).

activities.title: Plot and read on a four-quadrant grid
steps: Given a target coordinate such as (-3, 2), place a point by first moving horizontally along the x-axis to -3, then vertically along the y-axis to 2, and check whether it lands on target.

Immediately after plotting (-3, 2), plot (2, -3) and compare where the two points land: note that swapping the order of the two numbers (each keeping its own sign) sends the point to a visibly different quadrant.
Switch to reading: a point is shown already marked on the grid, and the learner states its coordinates as (x, y) with correct signs.
Repeat with on-axis points such as (0, 2) and with negative and fractional values so plotting and reading are both rehearsed.
State what one grid line is worth before each plot or read, practising with grids where each line represents 1, then 2, then 5.
activities.insight: The order of the two numbers and the sign of each carry independent meaning: (-3, 2) and (2, -3) are different points in different quadrants, and the interval each grid line represents must be checked before counting.

activities.title: Name the quadrant from the signs
steps: For a given point, state its quadrant by its sign pair: (+,+), (-,+), (-,-), (+,-), rather than recalling an abstract quadrant number.
Rehearse the convention against the origin (0,0): confirm that the first coordinate is read on the horizontal axis and the second on the vertical.
Classify on-axis points such as (0, 2): explain why a point with a zero coordinate sits on an axis and is not inside any quadrant.
activities.insight: The combination of signs locates which region of the plane a point lies in, and a zero coordinate places a point on an axis rather than inside a quadrant.

activities.title: Compare correct and incorrect readings
steps: Consider a dispute about a point plotted 8 units right of the origin and 6 units up: one person says it is (8, 6), another says (6, 8). Decide who is right and explain why, pointing to which number belongs on which axis.

Explain, using a case like plotting (4, -5), why 'along the corridor, up the stairs' is unreliable for negatives — here you go along then DOWN — and why 'read the first coordinate on the x-axis' always holds.
Predict where A(3, -2) and A(-2, 3) each land and justify whether they are the same point or different.
activities.insight: Reasoning about why a reading is right or wrong fixes the ordered-pair convention more durably than a first-quadrant mnemonic, which fails once the y-coordinate is negative.

activities.title: Accuracy check across all four quadrants
steps: Plot and label a set of points spanning every quadrant plus an on-axis case, e.g. A(3, -2), B(-4, 1), C(-2, -3), D(0, 2).
Read back the coordinates of points already marked on the grid, including on a non-unit scale (axes rising in 2s).
Describe how a point moves when a coordinate changes sign, e.g. B from (-4, 1) to (-4, -1): which direction and how far.
activities.insight: Fluency means plotting from coordinates AND reading coordinates from a plotted point reliably, including negative, on-axis, and non-unit-scale cases (fractional values are practised in the first activity).

checkQuestion: Here is a coordinate grid showing all four quadrants, with each square worth one unit. Plot and label these four points: A(3, -2), B(-4, 1), C(-2, -3), D(0, 2). When you have finished, I will point to a fifth point already marked on the grid (drawn on axes that go up in 2s) and you tell me its coordinates.
checkAnswer: A sits in the fourth quadrant (3 right, 2 down); B in the second (4 left, 1 up); C in the third (2 left, 3 down); D on the y-axis, 2 above the origin. The read-back point is named as (x, y) with correct signs and read against the '2s' scale (e.g. a point 3 lines right and 2 lines up is (6, 4)).
